Demographics: 15-month-old female
Chief complaint: high-grade fever and progressive weakness of both legs with difficulty in balance for two weeks
History of present illness: The child developed a high fever lasting two weeks together with gradually worsening weakness in both lower limbs, making it hard to maintain balance. There was no history of trauma. The family history is notable for consanguineous parents. On examination a small tuft of hair was seen in the midline over the mid-lumbar region. MRI of the brain and entire spine was obtained, revealing two separate Type 1 split cord malformations in the thoracolumbar spine separated by bony spurs, as well as a midline tract at L1 and a purulent collection in the epidural space extending from T12 to L3. Laboratory workup showed an elevated C-reactive protein. The patient underwent surgical excision of the midline tract and drainage of the purulent collection, followed by a course of intravenous antibiotics. Neurological function improved postoperatively. Four weeks later, a second operation was performed to address the split cord malformations, with removal of the bony spurs and reconstruction of the dural sheath. The postoperative course was uneventful and lower-extremity strength returned to normal.
Past medical history: unremarkable birth history
Exposures risk factors: consanguineous parents
Physical exam findings: Power left lower limb 3/5; Power right lower limb 4/5; Midline tuft of hair over mid-lumbar region, no obvious opening
Lab findings: C-reactive protein 2.8; CT abdomen/pelvis: duplicate collecting system with two separate renal pelvises and ureters in the right kidney; Culture of purulent material: gram-positive organism resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics
Imaging findings: MRI brain and full spine: two separate Type 1 split cord malformations in the thoracolumbar region (T4-T6 and T9-T11) separated by bony spurs, with the hemicords reuniting into a single cord at lower levels; MRI: midline tract extending to the dura at L1; MRI: purulent collection in the epidural space from T12 to L3; CT kidney, ureter, bladder: duplicate collecting system with two separate renal pelvises and ureters on the right side

The mass is located anterior to the lumbar spine and sacrum, displacing adjacent abdominal contents superiorly. The lumbar vertebrae and spinal canal are visible posteriorly. The lumbar vertebrae and intervertebral discs are visible posteriorly.; An intraoperative photograph showing a surgical field with exposed soft tissues and anatomical structures. Demographics: 65-year-old male
Chief complaint: Occipital headache of 1-week duration
History of present illness: The patient developed a one-week history of occipital headache without fever. Neurological examination on presentation was normal and routine laboratory tests were within normal limits. Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral occipital lesions: the central portion was hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, while the peripheral rim was isointense on T1 and hypointense on T2. Diffusion-weighted imaging showed a hyperintense region within the central cavity, and post-contrast images revealed a ring-enhancing lesion after administration of gadolinium-DTPA. Whole-body CT identified small nodules in the lingular segment of the left lung. The patient underwent left occipital craniotomy with intra-operative ultrasound guidance, revealing a pseudo-encapsulated firm mass; yellowish-white material was aspirated from the cavity and the adherent capsule was resected. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient received intravenous ceftriaxone followed by oral therapy. Follow-up MRI and thoracic CT performed five months later showed complete resolution of the intracranial lesion and the pulmonary nodule.
Past medical history: autoimmune hemolytic anemia; chronic prednisolone therapy (10 mg/day)
Exposures risk factors: long-term corticosteroid use leading to immunosuppression
Physical exam findings: afebrile; normal neurological examination
Lab findings: normal admission laboratory tests
Imaging findings: bilateral occipital lesions with central hypointensity on T1 and hyperintensity on T2; peripheral rim isointense on T1 and hypointense on T2; diffusion-weighted imaging hyperintense region within central cavity; ring enhancement after gadolinium-DTPA administration; small nodules in the lingular segment of the left lung on chest CT; post-operative MRI confirming total resection of the left occipital lesion

In the left temporal-occipital region, there is a well-defined, ring-enhancing cystic lesion with a dark center and a bright, thin peripheral rim. A white lowercase letter "d" is located in the bottom-left corner of the image.; An axial T1-weighted contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain. Demographics: 69-year-old Japanese male
Chief complaint: Fever for 2 days
History of present illness: The patient experienced a slight fever (37.4 °C) and left lower abdominal pain one week prior to admission, which resolved after a few days. Two days before admission he developed a higher fever (38.8 °C) persisting despite antipyretics. On admission he reported no other symptoms. Physical exam was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed marked leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers. Imaging demonstrated multiple low-echoic focal hepatic lesions and an intravascular filling defect in the right branch of the portal vein, as well as colonic diverticula with wall thickening. Blood cultures later grew gram-positive cocci. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and anticoagulation, with gradual clinical and laboratory improvement and resolution of imaging abnormalities over the following months.
Past medical history: Hypertension
Exposures risk factors: Losartan 25 mg/day; Benidipine 4 mg/day; Immunocompetent; Nonsmoker; No alcohol use
Physical exam findings: Temperature 38.8 °C; Blood pressure 128/80 mmHg; Heart rate 92 beats/min regular; Oxygen saturation 98%; Partial pressure of oxygen 94.3 Torr; No significant abnormalities on chest and abdominal examination; Normal chest X-ray; Normal abdominal X-ray; Normal electrocardiogram
Lab findings: White blood cell count 18.2 ×10^9/L (high); Alanine transaminase 58 U/L (slightly elevated); Alkaline phosphatase 559 U/L (elevated); Gamma-glutamyltransferase 274 U/L (elevated); C-reactive protein 20.98 mg/dL (elevated); Plasma fibrinogen 766 mg/dL (elevated); Prothrombin time-INR 1.33 (slightly elevated); Fibrin/fibrinogen degradation products 6.1 µg/mL (elevated); D-dimer 2.1 µg/mL (elevated); Hemoglobin A1c 5.5% (normal); Urinalysis normal
Imaging findings: Abdominal ultrasonography: multiple low-echoic, irregularly shaped focal hepatic lesions in segments 5 and 6, no surrounding capsule, no flow on color Doppler; mild enlargement of right hepatic lobe; mild fatty liver; bilateral renal cysts; Contrast-enhanced dynamic abdominal CT: intravascular filling defect in right branch of portal vein; multiple colonic diverticula; thickened wall of sigmoid colon; slightly homogeneous enhancement of a hepatic lesion in segment 6 during equilibrium phase; Colonoscopy (day 21): multiple diverticula and localized wall stiffness adjacent to sigmoid diverticula suggesting prior inflammation

The image includes a depth scale on the right side ranging from 0 to 15 cm.; An axial contrast-enhanced CT scan of the upper abdomen shows the liver, spleen, and stomach. A white arrow points to a small, low-attenuation filling defect within a branch of the portal vein in the liver. Demographics: 7-month-old male infant, born preterm at 32 weeks gestation, birth weight 1.6 kg
Chief complaint: Swelling in the right thigh
History of present illness: The infant was born preterm (32 weeks) and did not receive BCG vaccination at birth. At 2 months of age, when he weighed 2 kg, he was given a full vial of BCG vaccine (approximately ten times the usual dose) intramuscularly into the right thigh instead of the standard intradermal dose in the arm. Five months after the injection (approximately at 7 months of age), a swelling developed in the right thigh. The swelling was not associated with fever, weight loss, feeding difficulties, or failure to thrive. Developmental milestones were delayed by 2–3 months, attributed to prematurity.
Past medical history: Preterm birth at 32 weeks gestation
Exposures risk factors: High-dose intramuscular BCG vaccination administered to right thigh
Physical exam findings: Swelling of right anterolateral thigh, 4 cm × 5 cm, non-tender, diffuse margins, located in intramuscular plane; No palpable lymph nodes except small sub-occipital nodes considered insignificant; Other systemic examinations within normal limits
Lab findings: Complete blood count within normal limits; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate unremarkable; Chest radiograph normal
Imaging findings: MRI of right thigh shows an intramuscular lesion in the vastus intermedius muscle measuring 7.5 cm × 2.8 cm

History of present illness: The patient had a recent lumbar epidural steroid injection for a symptomatic disc herniation. Over the subsequent weeks she developed constipation, increasing pain in both legs, and a progressive inability to ambulate. This was followed by an episode of acute urinary retention. The symptoms worsened despite conservative measures, prompting urgent medical evaluation.

Demographics: 71-year-old male
Chief complaint: intermittent fever, chills, generalized weakness, myalgia, dysuria, and intermittent right-sided subcostal pleuritic pain for two weeks
History of present illness: The patient reported a two-week history of intermittent fever and chills associated with generalized weakness, malaise, and muscle aches. He also noted dysuria and intermittent right-sided subcostal pleuritic pain. He denied diarrhea, melena, recent travel, or sick contacts. On presentation he was hypotensive with systolic pressures in the 70s–80s, which responded to fluid resuscitation. He remained afebrile (36.7 °C) in the emergency department. Initial evaluation showed marked leukocytosis and acute kidney injury. Urinalysis was notable for pyuria. Imaging revealed heterogeneous hepatic lesions with surrounding fluid collections and diverticulosis of the colon. Over the subsequent hospital days the hepatic lesions enlarged, new intra-abdominal fluid collections appeared, and portal venous flow abnormalities were observed. He ultimately required surgical exploration, which identified multiple intra-abdominal fluid collections, adhesions, and a fistulous connection between the sigmoid colon and bladder. Post-operative recovery was uncomplicated.
Past medical history: hypertension; arthritis; benign prostatic hyperplasia; osteoarthritis
Exposures risk factors: no recent travel; no known sick contacts
Physical exam findings: temperature 36.7 °C; initial systolic blood pressure 70-80 mmHg, improved to 98/52 mmHg after fluids; pulse 90 bpm; respiratory rate 18/min, SpO₂ 98% on room air; anictic appearance; clear lung fields on auscultation; normal cardiac exam; soft abdomen with active bowel sounds, no tenderness, guarding, or rigidity in right upper quadrant; no costovertebral angle tenderness
Lab findings: WBC 36.6 × 10³/µL with 7% bands; creatinine 2.1 mg/dL; BUN 54 mg/dL; AST 84 U/L; ALT 51 U/L; alkaline phosphatase 182 U/L; total bilirubin 2.5 mg/dL; direct bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL; albumin 1.7 g/dL; total protein 5.5 g/dL; PT 15.1 seconds; PTT 38 seconds; INR 1.5; urinalysis: large leukocyte esterase, pyuria >60 HPF
Imaging findings: Abdominal ultrasound: heterogeneous liver lesions; CT abdomen/pelvis: multiple low-density liver lesions with enhancing rims and surrounding perihepatic fluid collections; diverticulosis noted in colon; Repeat CT after percutaneous drainage: enlargement of hepatic lesions, new interloop fluid collections in right mid abdomen and pelvis; Post-operative CT (6 days after surgery): decreased size of hepatic lesions, no new intra-abdominal fluid collections
Image findings: An axial contrast-enhanced CT scan of the upper abdomen. The image shows a large, heterogeneously hypodense mass occupying a significant portion of the right lobe of the liver. The gallbladder is visible and appears distended. The spleen, pancreas, and kidneys are also visualized in the abdominal cavity.

Demographics: 50-year-old female
Chief complaint: multiple palpable nodules in the right breast
History of present illness: The patient was hospitalized for 68 days in spring 2020 for severe COVID-19 infection complicated by respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation, acute kidney injury, bacteremia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and an upper gastrointestinal bleed. After recovery and discharge in late May 2020, she noted in August 2020 several tender, non-draining nodules in the right breast without warmth or erythema. Imaging studies (mammography, ultrasound, MRI) identified multiple oval, well-circumscribed masses extending toward the axilla and upper arm, some with rim enhancement and heterogeneous internal texture. A mildly enlarged right axillary lymph node with focal cortical thickening was also visualized. She elected surgical excisional biopsy of the most symptomatic lesions, which were removed and sent for pathology.
Past medical history: hypertension; hyperlipidemia; diabetes mellitus; tetralogy of Fallot with bioprosthetic valve; bilateral subpectoral silicone breast implants (placed 2013); severe COVID-19 infection with hospitalization in spring 2020
Exposures risk factors: recent severe COVID-19 infection with prolonged mechanical ventilation and broad-spectrum antibiotics; presence of silicone breast implants

Lab findings: Cultures from excised tissue negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal organisms
Imaging findings: Mammography: multiple oval masses in the right breast, equal density, well-circumscribed margins; Ultrasound: oval, parallel masses with heterogeneous internal echotexture in the right breast extending into axilla and upper arm; MRI: multiple rim-enhancing masses with intrinsic T1 and T2 hyperintensity in the right breast, mild right axillary node enlargement noted

Demographics: 73-year-old male
Chief complaint: dark amber-colored urine for the past 2 weeks
History of present illness: The patient developed flu-like symptoms with fever after receiving a COVID-19 booster and influenza vaccination 14 days ago, which resolved in five days. Shortly thereafter, he noticed his urine becoming dark amber. He denied dysuria or visible blood in the urine. Over the next several days he experienced generalized weakness and decreased oral intake. He was advised to increase fluid intake and obtain laboratory testing, which revealed elevated liver enzymes, prompting presentation to the emergency department.
Past medical history: horseshoe kidney with chronic kidney disease stage 3; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension; coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting and percutaneous intervention; abdominal aortic aneurysm status post endovascular repair

Demographics: 78-year-old male
Chief complaint: weakness, urinary incontinence, confusion, and poor oral intake
History of present illness: The patient was noted to be weaker on the left side than his baseline and presented to the emergency department as a stroke code. Computed tomography of the head showed no acute stroke. Vital signs showed a heart rate of 94 beats per minute and a respiratory rate of 31 breaths per minute. He was admitted for systemic infection workup and possible toxic, metabolic, or infectious insults. Empiric antibiotics were started and later narrowed after blood cultures grew gram-negative bacilli resistant to ampicillin and susceptible to ceftriaxone. Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large cystic lesion with an air-fluid level in the left hepatic lobe. Percutaneous drainage yielded purulent fluid that grew the same gram-negative organism. Serology was positive for Entamoeba histolytica antibodies, suggesting current or prior exposure. After completing the initial antibiotic course, additional antimicrobial therapy was initiated to address the extra-luminal parasitic infection.
Past medical history: hypertension; diabetes mellitus; paroxysmal atrial fibrillation; stroke with residual left-sided deficit; waxing and waning mental status
Exposures risk factors: origin from China; long-term residence in the United States; no recent travel; no known prior diagnosis or treatment for Entamoeba infection
Physical exam findings: left-sided weakness greater than baseline; heart rate 94 beats per minute; respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute
Lab findings: blood cultures: gram-negative bacilli, ampicillin-resistant, ceftriaxone-susceptible; serum Entamoeba histolytica antibody positive by ELISA
Imaging findings: head CT: no acute intracranial abnormality; abdominal/pelvic CT: large cystic region with air-fluid level in the left lobe of the liver

Demographics: 69-year-old male
Chief complaint: nausea and gait disorder
History of present illness: The patient initially sought medical attention for exertional dyspnea, lower-extremity edema, hypertension, proteinuria, hematuria, and bilateral pleural effusion on chest X-ray. Laboratory testing showed elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibody (218.5 IU) and reduced complement levels (C3 51 mg/dL, C4 12.3 mg/dL). He was hospitalized, received high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone and tacrolimus, followed by oral prednisolone, tacrolimus, and azathioprine, and was discharged after six months. One year later he presented with nausea and dizziness; brain imaging demonstrated a multilocular cystic lesion with surrounding edema in the right parietal lobe, appearing ring-enhancing on contrast MRI. He underwent stereotactic burr-hole drainage; intra-operative fluid showed Gram-positive filamentous bacteria, later identified as Nocardia species. Post-operatively he received meropenem, initially combined with vancomycin, which was stopped after organism identification. Due to renal function decline, meropenem dose was reduced and later switched to ceftriaxone. Over the ensuing weeks his neurological status worsened, and he developed urinary tract infection and bloodstream infection with gram-positive bacilli and an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae. Despite antimicrobial therapy his condition deteriorated, and he died after a prolonged hospital stay. Autopsy revealed micro-abscesses in lung, heart valve, liver, and kidney, with filamentous and yeast-like fungi present in multiple organs.
Past medical history: hypertension; proteinuria; hematuria; leukopenia; family history of similar autoimmune condition in daughter
Exposures risk factors: no history of smoking; no alcohol use; no recent travel; no outdoor activities; no sexual activity; immunosuppressive therapy (tacrolimus, azathioprine, prednisolone); indwelling urinary catheter during hospitalization
Physical exam findings: blood pressure elevation; lower-extremity edema; dyspnea on exertion; decreased level of consciousness later in course
Lab findings: anti-double-stranded DNA antibody 218.5 IU; complement C3 51 mg/dL; complement C4 12.3 mg/dL; proteinuria (quantitative not specified); hematuria (quantitative not specified); leukopenia (cell count not specified); Gram-positive filamentous bacteria seen on Kinyoun stain from brain lesion fluid; blood cultures positive for extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacteriaceae; inflammatory markers improved over time; renal function declined during hospitalization
Imaging findings: chest X-ray showing bilateral pleural effusion; brain CT demonstrating low-density area in right parietal lobe; contrast MRI showing multilocular, ring-enhancing cystic lesion in right parietal lobe; follow-up brain CT showing gradual reduction in size of the lesion

Demographics: 85-year-old male
Chief complaint: Anorexia, fatigue, headache, and shortness of breath for 2-3 weeks
History of present illness: The patient experienced 2–3 weeks of anorexia, fatigue, headache, and dyspnoea. Prior to admission he received oral penicillin for seven days for presumed pneumonia without improvement. He was admitted and initially treated intravenously with penicillin G and gentamicin for suspected pneumonia and endocarditis; chest X-ray and echocardiography were normal. Blood and urine cultures obtained after antibiotics showed no growth. Due to poor clinical response, antibiotics were changed to intravenous mecillinam on day 7 and then to cefuroxime on day 9. Elevated alkaline phosphatase prompted abdominal ultrasound and CT on day 14, which revealed a large right-lobe liver abscess (≈10.5 × 7.2 × 8.7 cm). Ultrasound-guided drainage removed purulent material; antibiotics were stopped after two days and the patient was discharged without further therapy. One hundred nine days later he collapsed at home and was readmitted. Empiric therapy with cefuroxime, later supplemented with gentamicin, was started for suspected urosepsis. Liver ultrasound showed no abscess, but blood cultures grew an organism; a repeat CT scan identified a new ≈2 cm liver abscess adjacent to the prior lesion, while the original area had decreased to ≈3 cm and appeared hypodense. Ten days after admission, oral ciprofloxacin was administered for 41 days. After completing antibiotics, weekly blood tests showed normal CRP and leukocyte counts, and he was declared infection-free. At eighteen-month follow-up he remained well with no relapse.
Past medical history: Pacemaker implantation one year prior for third-degree atrioventricular block
Exposures risk factors: No recent foreign travel; No known contact with individuals from Southeast Asia; Recent use of multiple antibiotics (penicillin, mecillinam, cefuroxime, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin); Implanted cardiac device (pacemaker)

Demographics: 40-year-old male

On arrival he was febrile (39.5 °C), hypotensive (systolic BP 84 mmHg), tachycardic (110 bpm), and had an altered level of consciousness. Physical exam showed neck stiffness, decreased skin turgor, and no focal neurological deficits or visual complaints. Initial labs demonstrated leukocytosis (11,600/µL), elevated CRP (12.1 mg/L), elevated total protein (9.6 g/dL), renal impairment (creatinine 1.54 mg/dL), severe hyponatremia (116 mEq/L) and hyperkalemia (7.3 mEq/L). CT of the head and body revealed only enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed modestly increased protein (66.5 mg/dL), IgG (14.6 mg/dL), and leukocyte count (56/µL, predominantly monocytes), with normal glucose. Empiric antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal agents were started. Electrolyte disturbances persisted, prompting evaluation of adrenal and pituitary function, which revealed abnormalities suggesting hormonal insufficiency; hormone replacement therapy was initiated, leading to normalization of electrolytes. Subsequently the patient developed large-volume polyuria (3–8 L/day) and intense thirst; a synthetic antidiuretic agent was prescribed. MRI of the brain demonstrated an irregularly enlarged sellar region, loss of the normal posterior T1 hyperintensity, thickened sphenoid sinus mucosa, and a ring-enhancing lesion with diffusion restriction, consistent with a collection within the gland. Antibiotic therapy was adjusted to a drug with better central nervous system penetration and continued for several weeks, during which imaging improvement was noted. At two-year follow-up the patient remains on chronic hormone supplementation.

Demographics: 44-year-old female

History of present illness: The patient experienced a 12-day course of fever accompanied by abdominal pain radiating toward the epigastrium. She had a known history of gallstones. She underwent open gallbladder removal and exploration of the bile duct; intra-operative findings confirmed the above imaging results. Six days after discharge she returned with a three-day history of subjective fever and dysuria; suprapubic palpation was mildly tender. Laboratory testing showed leukocytosis (11,400 / mm³) with neutrophil predominance and urinalysis revealed many white blood cells and positive leukocyte esterase. WBC rose to 13,200 / mm³ with a left shift; urinalysis was now normal. Empiric antibiotics were escalated. Despite resolution of urinary symptoms, fever persisted. Repeat ultrasound excluded intra-abdominal fluid collections and confirmed proper drain placement. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated. Because fever continued, abdominal CT was performed, which showed diffuse inflammation of the right iliopsoas muscle with a 15 mL fluid collection. Percutaneous drainage yielded purulent material, and the patient’s condition improved rapidly, with fever resolving. She was discharged after a week of hospitalization.

Demographics: 33-year-old female

History of present illness: The patient is an obese woman with end-stage kidney disease due to type 1 diabetes who received a deceased donor kidney transplant 6.5 months earlier. Physical exam was notable for alertness, orientation, and unremarkable lung and cardiovascular findings. Initial laboratory evaluation showed mild leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hyperglycemia, mild hyponatremia, normal potassium, low bicarbonate, and elevated creatine phosphokinase. Renal function was within baseline limits. Over the next five days his respiratory status deteriorated, with increased work of breathing, tachypnea, and oxygen saturation dropping to 87% on nasal cannula. He developed a non-oliguric decline in renal function, with rising serum creatinine and BUN, and arterial blood gas revealed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.25, HCO₃⁻ 13 mEq/L). Demographics: 60-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient with end-stage renal disease underwent dual kidney transplantation from an expanded criteria donor. Computed tomography angiography confirmed approximately 80% narrowing of the artery supplying the cranially positioned graft kidney, while the artery to the caudal graft was normal. A DTPA renal scan showed delayed radiotracer uptake in the cranial graft but preserved overall perfusion and cortical tracer uptake. Post-procedure Doppler at one year showed normalized flow velocities (PSV 150 cm/sec, EDV 110 cm/sec, renal-aortic ratio 3.1) with no evidence of in-stent restenosis. Blood pressure remained controlled on the same antihypertensive regimen. Two years later, the patient died from COVID-19-associated pneumonitis.

Demographics: 56-year-old male
Chief complaint: Severe shortness of breath and worsening oxygenation
History of present illness: The patient underwent an allogeneic bone-marrow transplant 11 months earlier and was maintained on an immunosuppressive regimen. Approximately one month before admission he developed a viral respiratory illness followed by increasing dyspnea and a flare of an underlying transplant-related complication, prompting re-initiation of immunosuppression and empirical antibiotics, antifungals, and antivirals. Despite these measures his respiratory status continued to deteriorate, leading to transfer to the intensive care unit where he was found to be tachypneic (respiratory rate 36/min) with low pulse-oximetry readings. Initial chest computed tomography showed bilateral peripheral patchy consolidations with diffuse ground-glass opacity. He was started on high-dose corticosteroids and non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation, but soon required intubation and mechanical ventilation because of severe hypoxemia and altered consciousness. Progressive ventilator asynchrony and poor lung compliance prompted initiation of venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Bronchoalveolar lavage performed after ECMO initiation did not reveal any active pulmonary infection. An immunomodulatory agent was added to the regimen together with continued corticosteroids. Over the next several days his oxygenation improved and radiographic infiltrates resolved, allowing weaning from ECMO and extubation. Shortly after extubation he developed a worsening cough, drop in oxygen saturation, and radiographic worsening of bilateral infiltrates. Laboratory testing demonstrated positivity for a viral antigen, and despite antiviral therapy and continuation of the immunomodulatory agent his respiratory failure progressed, necessitating re-intubation. He subsequently developed type II respiratory failure and died on ICU day 22.
Past medical history: Nephrotic syndrome secondary to primary amyloidosis (remitted after melphalan-prednisone therapy); Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia; Allogeneic bone-marrow transplantation
Exposures risk factors: Allogeneic bone-marrow transplantation; Prolonged immunosuppressive therapy (cyclosporine, corticosteroids)

Demographics: Male infant born at 26 weeks and 5 days gestational age, birth weight 1,100 g
Chief complaint: Premature infant requiring cardiac surgical intervention
History of present illness: The infant was born preterm with severe respiratory distress and was treated with surfactant, indomethacin and inotropic support. On day of life (DOL) 1, indomethacin therapy was started for a symptomatic congenital cardiac shunt lesion but was ineffective, and the infant was transferred on DOL 3 for cardiac surgical repair, which was performed without immediate complications. Enteral feeding with formula began on DOL 4 and unpasteurized breast milk was added on DOL 7. However, feeding intolerance and abdominal distension persisted, leading to cessation of feeds on DOL 7. Hyperosmolar enemas were given with limited effect. On DOL 8, bilious gastric residuals were noted and abdominal radiography revealed free intraperitoneal air. An emergent laparotomy identified a perforation of the terminal ileum, which was resected and an ileostomy created. Post-operative feeding difficulties and rising hepatic transaminases occurred from DOL 14 onward. On DOL 17, recurrent abdominal distension prompted repeat imaging, again showing free intraperitoneal air. A second laparotomy uncovered another perforation proximal to the ileostomy, which was repaired. The infant subsequently recovered, with resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms, closure of the ileostomy at three months of age, and discharge at five months with no neurodevelopmental sequelae reported at five-year follow-up.
Past medical history: Prematurity (26 weeks gestation); Respiratory distress syndrome; Symptomatic congenital cardiac shunt lesion; Indomethacin therapy; Inotropic support with dopamine and dobutamine
Exposures risk factors: Prematurity; Low birth weight; Use of indomethacin; Use of inotropic agents

Demographics: 60-year-old female
Chief complaint: Low level of consciousness
History of present illness: The patient attempted suicide and was brought to the emergency department with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 11, reporting dizziness and drowsiness after ingesting substances. Urine testing identified the presence of amphetamines and benzodiazepines. Over the next two days her level of consciousness deteriorated, with GCS decreasing to 9 and then to 3. She required therapeutic hemodialysis to aid drug clearance. On the third day she developed severe abdominal distension, absence of bowel sounds, and no passage of stool. Imaging revealed complex fluid collections in the abdomen, prompting an emergent laparotomy that identified a defect in the stomach wall and widespread intra-abdominal inflammation, which were surgically repaired and drained. Two weeks later she experienced recurrent abdominal distension, constipation, ascites, and peripheral edema. Repeat imaging showed persistent multiloculated fluid collections, leading to a second laparotomy. Post-operative course was complicated by worsening renal function, coagulation abnormalities, and systemic infectious signs, culminating in cardiac arrest and death.

Demographics: 10-year-old girl
Chief complaint: persistent headache progressing to fourth cranial nerve palsy with vertical diplopia
History of present illness: The patient underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. At day +164 she developed a persistent headache and fatigue, with high blood viral loads; treatment was switched to treatment. Despite clearance of virus from blood, the headache worsened. Demographics: 54-year-old male

Demographics: 61-year-old female
Chief complaint: ocular pain and visual impairment of the left eye persisting for 2 weeks
History of present illness: The patient had a known history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy in both eyes and cystoid macular edema in the left eye. She received an intravitreal bevacizumab injection in the left eye three weeks prior and underwent panretinal photocoagulation in both eyes two weeks prior, after which intraocular pressure in the left eye was treated with an anti-glaucoma agent. Two weeks after the laser treatment she noted worsening ocular pain and loss of vision in the left eye lasting for about two weeks. At presentation her left-eye vision was reduced to hand motion. Slit-lamp examination showed marked anterior chamber inflammation with 4+ cells and hyphema, along with iris neovascularization. Fundus examination was limited by dense vitritis and showed retinal vascular obliteration. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated delayed arterial filling suggesting ocular ischemia, while carotid Doppler was unremarkable. Because dense vitritis precluded detailed retinal assessment, a pars plana vitrectomy was performed, during which necrotizing retinitis with extensive retinal whitening and hemorrhage along the inferotemporal vascular arcade was observed, raising concern for an infectious process. Vitreous samples were sent for PCR and cultures. Subsequent follow-up over 12 months showed no recurrence of the retinal lesion, but the left eye remained without light perception due to optic nerve damage and persistent retinal ischemia.
Past medical history: well-controlled diabetes mellitus; proliferative diabetic retinopathy (both eyes); cystoid macular edema (left eye)
Exposures risk factors: intravitreal bevacizumab injection (left eye); panretinal photocoagulation (both eyes); recent ocular surgery (pars plana vitrectomy)

Demographics: 55-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit with a 10-day history of dyspnea, fever, and productive cough. A nasopharyngeal PCR test was positive for a viral respiratory pathogen (CT value 21). He required escalating oxygen support, progressing from a non-rebreather mask to high-flow nasal cannula and CPAP, and was intubated on hospital day 11. After a brief extubation, he required re-intubation on day 23 and was finally extubated on day 26. On day 27 he experienced a prolonged generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 10 minutes, which was terminated with intravenous midazolam. Subsequent seizures recurred on days 30 and 34, each lasting 2–3 minutes and responding to additional midazolam doses. Antiseizure medications were initiated and adjusted. An EEG showed generalized slowing suggestive of severe encephalopathy. Brain MRI demonstrated scattered left-dominant cortical gyriform hyperintensities on DWI/FLAIR, multiple punctate microbleeds in the corpus callosum and subcortical regions, and bilateral pachymeningeal enhancement without nodularity. Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid with a white blood cell count of 3/µL, red blood cell count of 2425/µL, protein >6 g/L, glucose 5.44 mmol/L, and a high copy number of cytomegalovirus DNA (103,614 copies). Cultures and broad viral panels were negative. Antiviral therapy was started, and repeat CSF later showed clearance of viral DNA. The hospital course was further complicated by fungal infections with Candida species and a secondary bacterial lung infection, requiring appropriate antimicrobial therapy. A tracheostomy was performed on day 48. Neurologic status gradually improved, leading to ventilation weaning, transfer to the ward on day 66, and subsequent rehabilitation with persistent limb weakness.

Demographics: 17-year-old Saudi male

Demographics: 66-year-old female

An aqueous sample was obtained for analysis. Subsequent management included antiviral therapy, topical steroids, and intraocular pressure-lowering agents, leading to controlled pressure and resolution of inflammation.

Demographics: 41-year-old male
Chief complaint: Left eye redness, blurred vision, ocular pain, and persistently high intraocular pressure
History of present illness: The patient has experienced approximately one left-eye episode per year for the past seven years, each characterized by redness, blurred vision, ocular pain, and intraocular pressure spikes to 30–60 mmHg despite use of maximal topical and systemic pressure-lowering medications. At the current evaluation his left-eye visual acuity was 6/18, relative afferent pupillary defect was absent, and intraocular pressure measured 56 mmHg while on dexamethasone, timolol, brimonidine, dorzolamide, latanoprost, oral acetazolamide 250 mg QID, and glycerol syrup. Slit-lamp exam showed anterior chamber cells graded 2+, fine keratic precipitates centrally, a white conjunctiva, and a clear cornea. Fundus examination revealed a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.9. Humphrey visual field testing and optical-coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fiber layer demonstrated advanced optic-nerve changes. Anterior chamber paracentesis was performed, and aqueous fluid was sent for PCR testing. After detection of viral DNA, antiviral gel therapy was initiated, and a glaucoma drainage device was implanted. Post-operatively, intraocular pressure stabilized between 7–14 mmHg without additional pressure-lowering agents and no further episodes were observed.

Demographics: 60-year-old female
Chief complaint: watery diarrhea, low-grade fever, nausea, and vomiting
History of present illness: The patient, a woman in her 60s with well-controlled type 2 diabetes, presented with a 3-week history of watery diarrhea, low-grade fever, nausea and vomiting. Initial labs showed leukocytosis, mild anemia, normal platelets, elevated inflammatory markers, hypoalbuminemia, and hypernatremia. Stool testing revealed markedly elevated fecal calprotectin and was negative for Clostridioides difficile toxin. Abdominal CT demonstrated diffuse small-intestinal wall thickening and mucosal enhancement. Empiric intravenous antibiotics were started, but diarrhea and vomiting persisted for 5 days, leading to enteroscopy, which showed diffuse hyperemic and ulcerative mucosa in the jejunum and ileum. Within a few days, blood counts declined markedly, prompting adjustment of the antiviral regimen. Following the adjustment, counts improved, symptoms resolved, oral intake was resumed, and the patient was discharged on oral antiviral medication. Follow-up imaging and endoscopy one month later showed marked resolution with no active disease.

Demographics: 44-year-old woman
Chief complaint: persistent neck and back pain for over one year, recent worsening with numbness of both upper limbs and inability to move the neck
History of present illness: One year ago the patient presented with chronic neck and back pain. MRI showed destruction of the thoracic vertebrae (T11-T12) and CT revealed a lytic lesion of the right 12th rib. Surgical debridement and vertebroplasty were performed, and empirical anti-mycobacterial therapy was given despite negative biopsy. Six months later a postoperative wound collection required open debridement, which healed. One month before the current admission the pain recurred together with upper-extremity numbness and neck stiffness. Physical exam noted a healed 20 cm back incision, tenderness over cervical spinous processes, and increased muscle tone in the trapezius, rhomboid and sternocleidomastoid muscles. MRI demonstrated multiple cystic-appearing lesions at the craniocervical junction and fluid around the lumbar vertebrae; abdominal CT was unremarkable. Laboratory tests showed a mildly elevated white blood cell count with normal eosinophils and a mildly positive fecal occult blood test. Repeated cultures, puncture, cerebrospinal fluid analysis and histopathology were all negative for bacteria and mycobacteria. Metagenomic sequencing of the spinal fluid identified a high burden of reads from a parasitic organism, which was confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. An antiparasitic medication was started, leading to clinical improvement.
Exposures risk factors: no prior Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccination
Physical exam findings: healed 20 cm surgical wound on the back; tenderness and percussion pain over cervical spinous processes; increased muscle tone in bilateral trapezius, rhomboid, and sternocleidomastoid muscles; limited neck mobility
Lab findings: mildly elevated white blood cell count; normal eosinophil count; mildly positive fecal occult blood; negative bacterial and mycobacterial cultures from puncture and cerebrospinal fluid; negative histopathology for infectious organisms; negative PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Imaging findings: destruction of T11 and T12 vertebral bodies on MRI; lytic lesion of the right 12th rib on CT; multiple cystic-appearing masses at the craniocervical junction on MRI; fluid effusion around lumbar vertebrae on MRI; no abnormal findings on abdominal contrast-enhanced CT

Demographics: 16-year-old female
Chief complaint: two episodes of seizures
History of present illness: The patient had a one-year history of left-sided headache. She presented with two recent seizure episodes. Brain MRI with contrast demonstrated a well-defined, peripherally enhancing, rounded predominantly cystic lesion measuring approximately 5 × 4.9 × 4.8 cm in the left fronto-temporal region, containing multiple smaller cystic structures. There was surrounding peri-lesional edema causing mass effect, including effacement of the left ventricle and a 9 mm midline shift. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy showed increased lipid-lactate signal in the lesion. Chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound and liver enzyme tests showed no abnormalities. She underwent a fronto-temporal craniotomy with removal of the cystic lesion and intra-operative irrigation with hypertonic saline; antiparasitic medication was continued post-operatively. Post-operative CT demonstrated a calvarial defect at the surgical site and no residual intracranial lesion. Follow-up over six months showed the patient remained asymptomatic and seizure-free.

Demographics: 56-year-old female

Demographics: 6-year-old female
Chief complaint: abdominal pain, cough, fever, and vomiting
History of present illness: The patient presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain, cough, fever, and multiple episodes of vomiting. Initial evaluation in the emergency department noted fever, low oxygen saturation, and lung findings leading to a diagnosis of acute bacterial pneumonia and treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone and acetaminophen. Over the first hospital day she remained febrile, required increased oxygen, and developed a leg rash thought to be a drug reaction, prompting a chest CT that showed a cavitary lesion in the left lower lung suggestive of a complicated pneumonia with possible abscess. Antibiotics were switched to levofloxacin and vancomycin, and oral prednisone was added. Despite these measures, fever and inflammatory markers continued to rise, leading to transfer to a tertiary center. Re-evaluation noted persistent fever, productive cough, neutrophilia, and imaging that now revealed a cystic lesion in the liver and a cavitary lung lesion. Based on exposure history and imaging, a parasitic cystic process was considered, and antiparasitic medication was started alongside ongoing antibiotics. The patient subsequently underwent surgical resection of the lung cyst and recovered with continued postoperative care and eventual discharge.

Exposures risk factors: contact with three household dogs; residence in Ecuador

Imaging findings: chest X-ray: consolidation in left lung field; chest CT: cavitary lesion in left inferior lobe; abdominal ultrasound: cystic lesion in liver

Demographics: 38-year-old South African female
Chief complaint: progressive painless bilateral visual loss
History of present illness: The patient reported a gradual, painless loss of vision in both eyes beginning on 10 March 2020, accompanied by mild intermittent headaches relieved by simple analgesia. She had a known HIV infection diagnosed in 2006, initially started on antiretroviral therapy in 2012, with a switch to second-line therapy in 2020 after treatment default and virological failure. At presentation her HIV viral load was high and CD4 count was low. Ocular examination at that time showed bilateral intraocular inflammation with macular edema, disc pallor and non-perfused retinal vessels; she received topical and sub-Tenon's steroids and intravitreal injections, leading to resolution of macular edema. A systemic antimicrobial regimen was initiated after imaging abnormalities in the chest, after which her visual acuity continued to decline, ultimately resulting in no perception of light by May 2020. She was admitted again in February 2021 with improved HIV virologic control but persistent severe visual loss. Over the ensuing months she underwent additional intravitreal steroid therapy with transient reduction of intra-ocular fluid, but visual function remained absent and lenticular opacities developed.

Demographics: 31-year-old man
Chief complaint: headache, nausea, vomiting, confusion, and seizures with fever
History of present illness: The patient developed a three-day history of headache accompanied by nausea and vomiting, followed by five hours of confusion and two generalized tonic-clonic seizures. He also reported fevers up to 38.9 °C. There was no prior personal or family history of seizures. He has a history of acute myeloid leukemia treated with induction and consolidation chemotherapy, during which he also had a widespread papular rash with vesicles diagnosed as varicella. He received intravenous antiviral therapy at that time with complete resolution of skin lesions. On admission, vital signs showed a temperature of 37.5 °C. Neurologic examination demonstrated confusion, impaired extraocular movements (left eye adduction, right eye abduction), meningeal signs (neck stiffness, positive Kernig’s and Lesage’s signs), bilateral Babinski signs, and a palpable bladder. Initial head CT was unremarkable. Cerebrospinal fluid studies showed xanthochromic fluid with normal opening pressure, marked pleocytosis, and extremely high protein. Subsequent CSF cytology revealed a high proportion of atypical cells. MRI of the brain showed multiple cortical signal abnormalities with extensive pachymeningeal enhancement and irregular thickening; MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine demonstrated T2 hyperintense lesions at C2-C3 and T6-T9 with partial enhancement. Follow-up imaging showed gradual resolution of meningeal enhancement. Repeat CSF analyses later in the hospital course demonstrated decreasing cell counts and protein levels, and eventual normalization at six-month follow-up.

Demographics: 66-year-old female
Chief complaint: suspected left leg deep vein thrombosis
History of present illness: The patient developed fever and left ankle pain five days before admission, followed by a painful, purpuric left leg. Laboratory testing on admission showed microhaematuria (26 erythrocytes per high-power field), marked haemoglobinuria and a mildly elevated serum creatinine (0.11 mmol/L). Blood cultures drawn on day 2 were negative. Fever and purpuric lesions persisted, and on day 7 empirical therapy with vancomycin and meropenem was started. Subsequent blood cultures on day 12 grew pleomorphic, filamentous, branching Gram-positive rods, later identified by 16S rRNA sequencing as Cellulosimicrobium cellulans. Repeated cultures on days 19 and 28 yielded the same organism intermittently. Despite antimicrobial therapy, fever and purpuric lesions continued, and renal function worsened (creatinine 0.32 mmol/L). A renal biopsy demonstrated immune-complex deposition with tubulointerstitial inflammation. High-dose prednisone was initiated, leading to improvement and discharge on day 84. On day 157 the patient returned with fever, mental confusion, hypotension and acute left-arm ischemia. Brain CT showed multiple ischemic regions and intraparenchymal hemorrhages; left-arm ultrasound demonstrated a brachial artery thrombosis. Blood cultures were again negative, and empiric vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam was started. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a periprosthetic cavity near the aortic valve suggestive of an abscess. A Tc-99m HMPAO white-blood-cell SPECT scan supported infection around the prosthetic valve with embolic phenomena. The patient deteriorated and died on day 170.

Demographics: 58-year-old female
Chief complaint: progressively decreased vision in the left eye over the past year
History of present illness: The patient reported a gradual decline in visual acuity of the left eye during the preceding year. Near visual acuity was markedly reduced (J10, approximately 20/65). She underwent clear lens extraction with intraocular lens implantation on July 10, 2015 without intraoperative complications. One day post-operatively she experienced blurred vision and ocular pain while using topical levofloxacin. Examination showed BCVA 20/40, conjunctival injection, corneal edema, and marked anterior chamber cellular reaction (4+). The following day visual acuity deteriorated to light perception, a hypopyon developed and vitreous opacity was noted. Vitreous and anterior chamber taps were obtained for culture. Despite topical fluoroquinolone therapy and intravitreal vancomycin and amikacin administered every two days, the hypopyon persisted. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated vitreous opacity. Because of progressive inflammation, a trans pars plana vitrectomy with anterior chamber irrigation was performed on July 13, 2015, during which diffuse vitreous haze without hemorrhage or retinal break was observed. The intra-ocular specimens grew Staphylococcus hyicus, which was susceptible to multiple antibiotics. The intra-ocular inflammation improved with combined intravitreal amikacin and vancomycin, and the patient was discharged on October 8, 2015 with counting-fingers vision. Demographics: 79-year-old male
Chief complaint: pain and reduced vision in the left eye
History of present illness: The patient presented five months after a penetrating keratoplasty with pain and decreased vision in the left eye following a freshwater exposure while hiking in a forest in the Dominican Republic. Initial examination showed inferior edema of the corneal graft without ulceration. He was started on topical moxifloxacin, fortified vancomycin, and fortified gentamicin. Two weeks later he developed an anterior chamber hypopyon with fibrin deposition, and ocular ultrasound showed intra-ocular inflammatory material. He then underwent pars plana vitrectomy with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime, after which the infection appeared to improve and the topical antibiotics were tapered. Three weeks post-operatively an ultrasound demonstrated separation of the retinal layers, for which a repeat vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade was performed. Over the next several weeks he developed recurrent endothelial plaques in the corneal graft that responded briefly to fortified topical antibiotics but recurred. Six weeks after the initial vitrectomy he noted renewed pain and was found to have inflammatory membranes in the anterior chamber, prompting an anterior chamber washout and intracameral vancomycin and amphotericin B. Cultures from an anterior chamber tap grew a multidrug-resistant gram-negative rod. He was referred to a tertiary center where he had light perception only vision and an intra-ocular pressure of 45 mmHg in the left eye. Examination revealed an opacified corneal graft with paracentral thinning, a retrocorneal plaque, and no view into the anterior chamber. He underwent removal of the graft, intra-ocular lens and capsular bag, repeat penetrating keratoplasty, intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime, and sub-Tenon’s triamcinolone injection. Pathology showed inflammation without organisms. Five months after surgery his vision improved to 20/350 with aphakic correction and intra-ocular pressure normalized to 10 mmHg, with a clear graft and no signs of active infection or inflammation.

Demographics: 22-year-old female

History of present illness: The patient underwent deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) for severe keratoconus, which was converted to penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) due to a large Descemet membrane perforation. The next day a whitish infiltrate appeared in the centre of the graft accompanied by a small hypopyon and vitreous opacity, and visual acuity declined to counting fingers. On day 3 her vision decreased to hand motion, the infiltrate worsened with severe corneal edema and anterior chamber exudate, while the fever improved. Five days after the initial surgery a repeat PKP was performed because the infection spread to the host cornea and the anterior chamber became opaque. Intraoperatively the iris was covered with an exudative membrane, the pupil was fixed, and the anterior lens capsule was opacified. After the repeat graft the ocular inflammation subsided, and systemic and intravitreal antibiotics were continued. Two weeks later vision was counting fingers improving to 20/1000 with pinhole, the graft was clear, and the anterior segment was quiet but a lens opacity remained. Five months later cataract extraction with intraocular lens implantation was performed. Six months after the initial surgery the aided visual acuity was 20/200, the cornea remained transparent without signs of rejection or infection, and a posterior capsule opacity limited retinal view.

History of present illness: Approximately three weeks before presentation the patient developed an insidious, pulsating bitemporal and bioccipital headache that worsened when supine, accompanied by nausea, intermittent diplopia, phonophobia, gait instability, and a noticeable decline in short-term memory and executive function. He sought care at a local emergency department where brain MRI showed left basilar leptomeningeal enhancement and a lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein, low glucose and a lymphocytic pleocytosis. He was treated with antibiotics and discharged, but his symptoms progressed. One week later he returned to the emergency department and was again discharged. About one week after this second discharge he experienced a sudden weakness of the left face and left arm with reduced speech output. He presented to our tertiary center, where he reported daily chills at 4 a.m. but no fever or other systemic complaints. Neurologic examination showed left lower-motor-neuron facial weakness, dysarthria and diffuse hyperreflexia with bilateral Hoffmann’s signs. Laboratory studies demonstrated profound hyponatremia, mild normocytic anemia, elevated inflammatory markers, coagulopathy (elevated INR and aPTT), and elevated total bilirubin. Cerebrospinal fluid was grossly bloody with markedly increased protein (534 mg/dL) and low glucose (26 mg/dL); repeat lumbar puncture remained hypercellular (393 nucleated cells/µL, 46% lymphocytes). Extensive infectious work-up (including PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycoplasma, Lyme disease and fungal antigen testing) was negative. Brain MRI confirmed extensive nodular leptomeningeal enhancement involving the left ventral medulla, pons, midbrain, left Sylvian fissure and pituitary infundibulum. CT of the chest revealed multiple small non-calcified pulmonary nodules, while whole-body FDG PET-CT was otherwise negative and abdominal CT showed only a tiny hepatic cyst. Because the etiologic work-up remained inconclusive, a left far-lateral occipital craniotomy with C1 laminectomy was performed, yielding thick arachnoid with visible fungal-appearing colonies that were sampled for pathology and culture.

Demographics: 55-year-old male
Chief complaint: Encephalopathy and worsening oxygen requirements several weeks after liver transplantation
History of present illness: Five weeks after orthotopic liver transplantation, the patient developed two days of altered mental status with sparse speech and disorientation, accompanied by increasing need for supplemental oxygen (4 L nasal cannula to keep saturation >92%). Neurologic examination was non-focal. Laboratory evaluation showed a normal white blood cell count, elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen compared with baseline, and a markedly elevated arterial ammonia level on arrival. He was admitted to the intensive care unit, received broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage, and underwent lumbar puncture, which demonstrated elevated opening pressure and yeast organisms on Gram stain. Empiric antifungal therapy was initiated, and renal replacement therapy was started for metabolic deterioration. Despite initial improvement in ammonia levels, the patient required mechanical ventilation, repeated large-volume CSF drainage, and eventually tracheostomy. Complications included persistent low platelet count, renal failure, and progressive necrotic changes in the spleen. Imaging identified ventricular enlargement and an intestinal leak at the duodenum. The clinical course was further complicated by persistent fevers, hemodynamic instability, and an abdominal leak, leading to a decision for comfort-focused care.

Demographics: 44-year-old Hispanic woman
Chief complaint: Found unresponsive at home
History of present illness: The patient was discovered unresponsive and brought to the emergency department. On arrival her temperature was 36.6 °C, heart rate 126 bpm, respiratory rate 26/min, blood pressure 160/90 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 78% on room air. She was intubated emergently. Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis, markedly elevated inflammatory marker, severe hyperglycemia, hypernatremia, acute kidney injury, and metabolic acidosis. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR. She received insulin infusion for glycemic control, antiviral therapy, systemic corticosteroids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics for a possible bacterial superinfection. Metabolic abnormalities improved over the first three days, but respiratory status deteriorated with worsening hypoxemia despite mechanical ventilation, requiring escalation of ventilatory settings, neuromuscular blockade, and prone positioning. Tracheal aspirate cultures later grew a gram-negative rod and a mold. Antifungal therapy was added, followed by a change in antibacterial coverage based on susceptibility testing. On hospital day 8, chest CT performed for worsening oxygenation revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities and multiple cavitary lesions in the right lung. Despite added antifungal agents, the patient’s ventilation/perfusion ratio continued to decline, prompting bronchoscopy on day 13. Endobronchial inspection showed extensive gray necrotic-appearing lesions with near-complete destruction of the left upper lobe and lingula; biopsies demonstrated pauciseptated hyphae consistent with a zygomycete on silver stain, and cultures grew several fungal species. Hemoglobin A1c measured at that time was 13 %. The patient’s condition continued to worsen, leading to renal replacement therapy and ultimately death on hospital day 17.

Exposures risk factors: no tobacco use; hospitalization with mechanical ventilation; broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure; SARS-CoV-2 infection

Demographics: 31-year-old female
Chief complaint: severe oropharyngeal ulceration with pain and difficulty swallowing, unable to eat solids
History of present illness: The patient experienced recurrent aphthous stomatitis beginning in infancy, with episodes occurring monthly and later more frequently. Early childhood was marked by multiple episodes of oral candidiasis treated with topical agents. She had a history of severe lower respiratory infection at age 7 requiring prolonged courses of various antibiotics and an antifungal agent, after which she recovered. Throughout childhood and adolescence she reported high fevers with infections, a tendency to develop oral stomatitis when receiving antibiotics, chronic eczema in flexural areas, and microcytic anemia with persistently low weight percentile. At ages 17–25 she had recurrent mucosal ulcers in the oropharynx and esophagus, intermittent fever, and elevated liver enzymes. Endoscopic evaluations showed ulcerative lesions throughout the esophagus with Candida patches and narrowing, and gastric/duodenal lymphatic stasis. Imaging studies over the years documented intermittent pulmonary infiltrates with patchy alveolar opacities, fine interstitial changes, and later calcified upper-lobe lesions. At age 25 she presented with numerous deep buccal ulcers (5–14 mm), facial papulopustular lesions, and weight loss (37 kg, 167 cm). Chest CT demonstrated numerous small nodular lesions in the left apical and posterior lung segments. Blood cultures grew alpha-hemolytic streptococci; a buccal swab culture was positive for a common skin bacterium. Serology for a dimorphic fungus showed the presence of specific antibodies. Initial therapy with antiviral, antibacterial, and antifungal agents did not improve symptoms. Subsequent treatment with an echinocandin antifungal and low-dose corticosteroid led to rapid clinical improvement, allowing resumption of oral intake and weight gain. Maintenance therapy with low-dose corticosteroid and weekly antifungal was continued for several months, with occasional relapses managed by short courses of the same agents.

Demographics: 80-year-old male
Chief complaint: Fatigue and absence of urine output
History of present illness: The patient had a long-standing history of chronic kidney disease and related anemia. Chest CT demonstrated a dense opacity in the middle of the right lung, multiple nodules, mild interstitial changes and a pleural effusion. During hospitalization his temperature rose to 38.2 °C on day 4, fluctuated thereafter, and he died on day 9 of admission.

Demographics: 63-year-old male
Chief complaint: confusion, tremors, and weakness for the past 3 days
History of present illness: The patient was brought to the emergency department after three days of increasing confusion, tremor-like movements, and generalized weakness. According to his sister, he was previously independent in daily activities but had become nonsensical and exhibited an ataxic gait. He has a past history of a fungal infection for which he previously received fluconazole (discontinued due to side effects) and later was prescribed an oral antifungal agent, which he was intermittently non-compliant with. On arrival he was mildly bradypneic, oriented only to self, and unable to follow commands. A full metabolic and infectious work-up was performed, which was largely unremarkable except for thrombocytopenia and a left-shifted white blood cell count. Imaging of the head showed ventricular enlargement with periventricular edema. CSF studies showed no growth on culture. He required multiple lumbar punctures for CSF drainage and eventually underwent placement of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt. His mentation and gait gradually improved over several weeks, allowing discharge to a skilled nursing facility while continuing antifungal therapy. He later returned with worsening mentation; repeat imaging demonstrated new right frontal hypodensity with a surrounding collection near the shunt catheter and re-accumulation of ventricular fluid. The shunt was removed, an external ventricular drain placed, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were started after cultures grew gram-negative rods later identified as Proteus species. An additional antifungal agent was continued, and a metronidazole-type medication was added for a presumed intra-abdominal source. Over the subsequent days his mental status fluctuated, with imaging later showing persistent ventricular enlargement and intraventricular gas. After multidisciplinary discussion, care was transitioned to hospice due to poor neurological recovery.
Past medical history: alcoholic liver cirrhosis; prior fungal infection
Exposures risk factors: chronic liver disease; previous antifungal therapy with intermittent adherence; placement of ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Physical exam findings: mild bradypnea; oriented to self only, unable to follow commands; ataxic gait; rest of exam unremarkable

Demographics: 34-year-old male
Chief complaint: occipital headache persisting for two months
History of present illness: Eight months prior the patient suffered head trauma from a physical assault resulting in a nasal bone fracture and deviation of the nasal septum. He experienced mild intermittent obstructive dyspnea thereafter. He has a long-standing history of smoking (20 cigarettes daily for 21 years) and chronic alcohol consumption (approximately 1 L of alcohol per week for 11 years). Two months before admission he began to have a persistent occipital headache. Over the following six weeks he developed behavioral changes, disruption of higher mental functions, retrograde and anterograde amnesia, echolalia, and visual hallucinations. Initial treatment with diazepam, pentoxifylline, diclofenac and phenytoenin produced no improvement. About one and a half months after symptom onset he developed acalculia and multiple apraxias, rendering him unable to perform daily activities and requiring family assistance. Subsequent therapy with amitriptyline, bromazepam, B-complex vitamins and additional phenytoenin was also ineffective. Three weeks later he manifested ataxic gait and received emergency treatment for presumed poisoning (benzodiazepines with flumazenil, gastric lavage and activated charcoal). Within a week he rapidly lost the ability to sit up, exhibited psychomotor agitation, myoclonic movements triggered by loud sounds or light, spastic limb tonicity, and alternating states of soporose and awakened consciousness, eventually progressing to akinetic mutism. He was admitted to a regional hospital where empiric antibiotics (cefotaxime and metronidazole) were started for a possible neuroinfection, without clinical improvement, and was subsequently transferred to a tertiary unit for further evaluation.

Demographics: 68-year-old male
Chief complaint: acute visual loss in both eyes
History of present illness: The patient had chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b with advanced cirrhosis, leading to liver transplantation. Post-transplant immunosuppression initially included tacrolimus, which was replaced by cyclosporine because of confusion, along with mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone. Four months after transplantation he experienced sudden bilateral visual loss. Visual acuity was reduced (0.6 right eye, 0.12 left eye) with a relative afferent pupillary defect in the right eye. Fundoscopy showed bilateral optic disc edema with hemorrhages at the disc margin. Immunosuppression was modified (cyclosporine stopped, prednisolone increased). Vision partially improved over the next month but optic disc edema resolved and optic nerves became pale. Visual field testing demonstrated central scotomas. Brain MRI was normal. HCV viral load rose markedly. Over the subsequent months the patient received various antiviral regimens (peginterferon alpha-2a plus ribavirin, then ribavirin plus sofosbuvir, later daclatasvir plus sofosbuvir) while immunosuppression was adjusted. Visual acuity and visual fields showed modest fluctuation, with gradual improvement as liver function normalized and viral load decreased to undetectable levels.
Past medical history: chronic hepatitis C infection (genotype 1b); cirrhosis; liver transplantation; immunosuppressive therapy (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisolone)
Exposures risk factors: solid organ transplantation; immunosuppression with cyclosporine and other agents; high hepatitis C viral load

Demographics: 41-year-old woman
Chief complaint: abdominal pain, diarrhea and fever
History of present illness: In July 2006 she developed abdominal pain, diarrhea and fever. Persistent symptoms led to hospitalization in August 2006, during which colonoscopy showed a cobblestone-like appearance of the sigmoid colon. She was started on infliximab and 6-mercaptopurine in September 2006, achieving symptom relief by week 10. Approximately one year later she experienced delayed-onset fever and joint pain thought to be hypersensitivity to infliximab. The final infliximab dose was given in October 2010 with normal liver enzymes. In December 2010 mild elevations of AST and ALT were noted before the first dose of adalimumab; the enzymes remained elevated after a second dose. On 4 January 2011 she felt generalized malaise and had marked increases in AST and ALT, prompting hospital admission. Further testing showed positive HBsAg, high viral DNA levels, genotype C, and negative anti-HCV antibodies. Imaging showed no chronic liver disease; liver biopsy demonstrated mild fibrosis. Antiviral therapy with entecavir was started on 5 January 2011, adalimumab was held after two doses, and granulocytapheresis was performed to maintain intestinal remission. Liver enzyme levels peaked on 14 January and then declined, returning to normal by 29 March 2011. By June 2011 viral DNA was undetectable, allowing re-introduction of adalimumab. She continued entecavir with sustained normal liver tests, and anti-HBs antibodies became positive after ten months of therapy, with ongoing adalimumab and no gastrointestinal symptoms.
Exposures risk factors: treatment with infliximab (anti-TNF); 6-mercaptopurine therapy; adalimumab therapy; granulocytapheresis; no known travel or occupational exposures

Demographics: 74-year-old male
Chief complaint: Altered mental status, fever, cough with mucopurulent sputum, and abdominal pain for 2 days
History of present illness: The patient developed fever, productive cough, abdominal pain and altered mental status over a two-day period. Physical examination revealed disorientation, livedo reticularis, increased capillary refill, bilateral rhonchi, and marked epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness with guarding. Initial laboratory studies demonstrated marked elevation of liver enzymes, high bilirubin, elevated lactate dehydrogenase, rising lactate, markedly increased C-reactive protein and procalcitonin, and leukocytosis with neutrophilia. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam) were started, and vasopressor support was initiated for circulatory instability. On the second hospital day his clinical condition worsened, prompting expansion of antimicrobial coverage to include vancomycin, metronidazole, and fluconazole. Demographics: 61-year-old male
Chief complaint: worsening malaise and abdominal pain
History of present illness: The patient resumed a BTK inhibitor for maintenance therapy of chronic lymphocytic leukemia and shortly thereafter experienced worsening malaise and abdominal pain. Over the next several months he developed symmetric paresthesias, first in the feet and fingertips and then progressing proximally above the knees. Neurological examination showed distal symmetric hypesthesia of the legs, reduced strength with atrophy of small muscle groups and gait disturbance. Nerve conduction studies were normal, but electromyography revealed acute and chronic denervation of lower-limb muscles and evoked potentials demonstrated central motor and sensory conduction abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed markedly elevated protein, modest pleocytosis and increased lactate. Initial high-dose methylprednisolone gave no improvement. Over three months his strength deteriorated further, especially in the upper limbs, reflexes became brisk with plantar extension, and sensory loss extended to the T5 level. Liver enzymes became elevated and viral RNA was detected at high levels in serum and later in CSF. Imaging showed slight cervical posterior funiculus involvement. Despite antiviral therapy, the patient experienced fluctuating viral RNA levels associated with adjustments in immunosuppressive therapy, leading to recurrent neurologic worsening, including bowel and urinary retention, and progressive thoracic spinal cord atrophy on MRI.

Demographics: 57-year-old male
Chief complaint: dry mouth, increased thirst, fatigue, and recent weight loss
History of present illness: The patient sustained a lumbar vertebral fracture in April 2021 and underwent surgical repair. During that hospitalization, laboratory testing revealed chronic viral infection of the liver and imaging showed liver structural changes consistent with advanced fibrosis, for which antiviral therapy was initiated. Follow-up imaging over the next two years demonstrated evolving hepatic lesions, including regenerative-appearing nodules and later multiple high-echogenic lesions. The patient declined further contrast MRI evaluation due to financial reasons. In June 2023 he was admitted for abdominal discomfort, distension, reduced appetite, dark urine, and occasional nausea. Imaging at that time identified additional liver lesions, prompting surgical resection of a portion of the liver and bile ducts, followed by postoperative recovery. He subsequently received systemic targeted therapy and an immune checkpoint inhibitor, and later underwent treatment of hepatic lesions. By early 2024 he experienced a rapid onset of severe hyperglycemia, marked polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Laboratory evaluation showed markedly elevated blood glucose levels, high glycated albumin and HbA1c, significant glucosuria, ketonuria, metabolic acidosis, and very low C-peptide concentrations. He required intensive insulin infusion, fluid resuscitation, and correction of acid-base abnormalities, after which he was transitioned to a basal-bolus insulin regimen and discharged with outpatient follow-up for glycemic management.

Demographics: 13-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient had end-stage renal disease due to bilateral renal hypoplasia and was on hemodialysis from 2014. Follow-up evaluations at 12 and 24 weeks after treatment cessation showed no recurrence of viral detection and no related adverse effects.

Demographics: 55-year-old male
Chief complaint: vomiting and stomach discomfort about 11 days after cellular immunotherapy infusion

Post-operative maintenance therapy was continued, and at nine-month follow-up there was no radiologic evidence of recurrence and tumor markers remained within normal ranges.

Demographics: 58-year-old female

Demographics: 26-year-old male

On 26 November, the patient presented with a 2-day history of stabbing waist and back pain, abdominal discomfort, edema of the limbs, and erythematous swelling with pruritus of the glans and prepuce. The next day he became unconscious, hypotensive (90/40 mmHg), bradycardic (39 bpm) and tachypneic, then suffered cardiac arrest requiring resuscitation. Post-resuscitation, he remained comatose on ventilatory support, with diffuse skin lesions ranging from vesicles to crusted pustules. Laboratory studies demonstrated severe anemia (Hb 1.6 g/dL), leukopenia (0.8 × 10⁹/L), neutropenia (0.6 × 10⁹/L), thrombocytopenia (9 × 10⁹/L), markedly elevated transaminases (AST 7360 U/L, ALT 9780 U/L), increased direct bilirubin (13.6 µmol/L), high serum creatinine (240.2 µmol/L), elevated D-dimer (>80 000 µg/L), positive plasma protamine paracoagulation test, and raised cardiac troponin I (1.78 ng/mL). Despite broad-spectrum anti-infection therapy, blood product transfusion, and intensive life-support measures, the patient died eight hours later.

Demographics: 34-year-old female
Chief complaint: 1-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen
History of present illness: The patient, at 4 weeks 5 days of amenorrhea, presented with a one-day history of epigastric pain radiating to the lower abdomen without other associated symptoms. She was afebrile with stable vital signs. Physical exam revealed epigastric tenderness; Murphy's and McBurney's signs were negative. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 13.54 (units) and a serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin level of 523 IU/L; C-reactive protein was not performed. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrated an empty uterine cavity, a 1.2 cm left adnexal structure with minimal vascularity posterior to the left ovary, and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Because of the short duration of amenorrhea, lack of vaginal bleeding, b-hCG level below the discriminatory zone, and empty uterus on scan, a diagnostic laparoscopy was offered. During laparoscopy, no hemoperitoneum or ectopic pregnancy was observed, but pus was noted in the pouch of Douglas originating from the tip of an inflamed appendix with evidence of rupture. The remainder of the pelvic and abdominal cavity appeared normal. Postoperatively, the patient received 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics and progesterone support. A transvaginal ultrasound on postoperative day 4 revealed an intrauterine gestational sac, and a follow-up scan three weeks later confirmed a viable 6-week pregnancy. Subsequent antenatal course was uneventful, culminating in delivery of a healthy infant by elective cesarean section at 38 weeks.

Demographics: 31-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient presented with an acute episode of severe abdominal pain and vomiting and was found to have obstruction of the biliary tract by gallstones, leading to emergency endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with placement of pancreatic and biliary stents. Demographics: 10-month-old female domestic shorthair cat
Chief complaint: progressive hindlimb weakness and gait abnormalities
History of present illness: The cat was taken into a rescue home and at 14 weeks of age was evaluated for poor weight gain, soft stool, and an upper respiratory infection with conjunctivitis, mucopurulent nasal discharge, and fever. The cat received a course of amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. At approximately 6 months the owner noted pelvic limb gait abnormalities that progressed over two weeks, with pain on palpation, reduced response on the right side, and right hindlimb paresis. Examination revealed symmetric pulses in both hind limbs. Laboratory testing at that time showed hypoalbuminemia, decreased albumin : globulin ratio, low creatinine, hyperphosphatemia, mild anemia, monocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and platelet clumping. By 8 months the cat showed worsening paraparesis, new thoracic limb stiffness, occasional urinary and fecal incontinence, a large easily expressible bladder, tetraparesis more severe in the pelvic limbs, tail paresis, and continued ataxia.
