Demographics: 48-year-old male
Chief complaint: Decreased vision, ocular pain, and photophobia in the right eye
History of present illness: The patient has congenital blindness with a phthisical left eye. One month prior he was riding a motorcycle when an insect-like foreign body struck his right eye. He presented to a primary hospital where the eye was irrigated and treated with 0.5% chloramphenicol eye drops for three days without relief. He then self-administered dexamethasone and neomycin eye drops purchased from a pharmacy, also without improvement. He sought care at a secondary hospital and was diagnosed with a corneal ulcer; he received oral acyclovir and 0.5% moxifloxacin eye drops for two weeks as an outpatient, but the lesion persisted. He was admitted and treated with fortified cefazolin and gentamicin eye drops. The condition worsened, prompting referral to a university ophthalmology department. On examination he had decreased vision, a whitish corneal infiltrate with feathery margins, satellite lesions, brown pigment on the temporal cornea, epithelial defect, corneal thinning, severe conjunctival injection, hypopyon, marked anterior chamber reaction, and reduced corneal sensation. Corneal scrapings were performed for Gram stain, KOH, calcofluor-white, bacterial and fungal cultures. KOH and calcofluor-white revealed numerous large septate hyphae. Initial Gram stain was negative. Fungal culture grew dematiaceous fungi, later identified by PCR as Exserohilum rostratum. He was started on hourly 5% natamycin eye drops, oral itraconazole, atropine, and levofloxacin, with discontinuation of the earlier antibiotics and antivirals. After one week there was no improvement; therapeutic corneal debridement and subconjunctival fluconazole were added. Over the next five weeks the infiltrate gradually resolved, leaving a corneal scar. Natamycin was switched to 2% ketoconazole eye drops due to cost, and treatment was continued for several weeks before discharge. At follow-up the scar remained stable, the anterior chamber was quiet, and best-corrected visual acuity improved to 6/12 in the right eye.

History of present illness: The patient underwent transepithelial photorefractive keratectomy (trans-PRK) for myopia in January 2020. Preoperatively he used 0.5% levofloxacin eye drops and 0.1% sodium hyaluronate drops four times daily for three days. Postoperatively he continued levofloxacin, sodium hyaluronate, and added 0.1% flumilon drops. On postoperative day 4 he noted soreness, redness, and reduced vision in the left eye. Visual acuity at that time was 12/20 (right) and 10/20 (left). The right corneal epithelium was mostly healed with some curling; the left cornea appeared cloudy centrally and infectious keratitis was suspected. He received intensive topical antibiotics (levofloxacin and lincomycin) but symptoms persisted. On postoperative day 6 he was transferred for further care. At presentation, the right eye showed poor epithelial healing; the left eye had bulbar conjunctival congestion, corneal edema, white infiltrates with unclear borders, an annular reaction ring, Descemet’s folds, and sediment on the endothelium. OCT showed central corneal swelling and cloudiness to about half the stromal depth. Confocal microscopy demonstrated necrotic and absent epithelial cells, stromal edema, blurred endothelium, numerous inflammatory cells in the superficial stroma, and highly reflective particles on the endothelium. Corneal scraping cultures grew colonies on blood agar after 36 h; Gram stain revealed Gram-positive cocci in short chains, non-hemolytic. Conjunctival sac smear with Giemsa stain showed many neutrophils and a few diplococci. After intensified topical antibiotic therapy the symptoms improved over the next few days.

Demographics: 16-year-old female
Chief complaint: Pain, redness, watering, and blurred vision in the right eye for 4 days
History of present illness: Four days prior to presentation the patient developed pain, redness, tearing, and decreased vision in the right eye. Fifteen days earlier she had experienced a fever accompanied by dysuria, a papulomacular rash over the lower abdomen and groin, and vague joint pains, for which she received symptomatic treatment elsewhere. She had been using topical antifungal and antibiotic eye drops in the right eye for two days before presentation. On examination she was found to have severe circumcorneal redness and a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate with an epithelial defect measuring about 6 mm x 6 mm. The anterior chamber was quiet with no hypopyon and the lens was phakic. Media opacity limited fundus view, with the optic disc faintly visible and the retina attached. Corneal sensations were intact in both eyes. Corneal scrapings were taken for microbiology. Systemic work-up, including blood cultures, inflammatory markers, autoimmune serologies, Mantoux test, chest radiograph, and abdominal-pelvic ultrasound, was performed to evaluate a possible systemic source. Blood culture grew a gram-negative bacillus identified as Klebsiella pneumoniae, which was later found to produce extended-spectrum beta-lactamase. Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated. After hospital admission, intravenous antibiotics were initiated based on susceptibility results. The ocular findings improved over the first week. One week later the patient developed new symptoms in the left eye, with a small stromal infiltrate and no epithelial defect; topical fortified antibiotics were continued. Subsequent follow-up showed resolution of the right-eye infiltrate and development of mild corneal edema, keratic precipitates, and anterior chamber cells in the left eye. After exclusion of other infectious and inflammatory causes, topical corticosteroids were added while continuing antibiotics. The patient later experienced a brief recurrence of ocular inflammation in the right eye following an isolated fever, which resolved with a short course of topical steroids.
Exposures risk factors: No history of ocular trauma, surgery, or contact lens use; Prior use of topical antifungal and antibiotic eye drops for 2 days; Recent systemic febrile illness with rash and joint pains

Demographics: 44-year-old male
Chief complaint: Acute onset ocular pain and photophobia in the right eye
History of present illness: Three days before presentation the patient sustained ocular trauma with a tree branch. Initial evaluation showed a temporal corneal epithelium erosion and a peripheral anterior stromal infiltration in the inferotemporal quadrant, measuring about 2 × 1.5 mm and staining with fluorescein. There was a mild anterior chamber reaction (Tyndall 1+, flare 1+). Empiric topical antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory drops were started. After four days the stromal infiltration resolved but the epithelial defect persisted, leading to placement of a therapeutic contact lens and continuation of selected drops. By day 15 the patient reported worsening symptoms; examination revealed a new paracentral corneal defect with a larger stromal infiltration (approximately 4.7 × 2.7 mm) in the inferior temporal region, accompanied by stromal disorganization on anterior segment OCT. Cultures were repeated and antifungal therapy was added while broad-spectrum antibacterial drops were discontinued. At day 25 fungal growth identified a pigmented filamentous organism. Targeted antifungal drops were continued, and antibacterial drops were modified. Over the following weeks the patient experienced progressive pain relief, improvement in visual acuity, and gradual reduction in the size of the corneal lesion, eventually leaving a small paracentral scar without active staining. Therapy was tapered and stopped by the fourth month with no adverse effects reported.
Past medical history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (24 years); Diabetic retinopathy; Chronic kidney disease; Renal-pancreatic transplant (5 years ago); Left eye low vision secondary to neovascular glaucoma
Exposures risk factors: Ocular trauma with a tree branch; Therapeutic contact lens use; Immunosuppression related to renal-pancreatic transplant
Physical exam findings: Right eye best corrected visual acuity 20/80; Left eye best corrected visual acuity hand motion; Temporal corneal epithelium erosion; Peripheral anterior stromal infiltration inferotemporal (initially 2 × 1.5 mm); Fluorescein staining of defect; Mild anterior chamber reaction (Tyndall 1+, flare 1+); Paracentral corneal defect with stromal infiltration (≈4.7 × 2.7 mm) on day 15; Moderate ciliary injection; Later small paracentral scar (leukoma) without staining

Demographics: 26-year-old male

Postoperatively, the patient received intensive topical chlorhexidine, tapered topical prednisolone, and short-course topical atropine. Visual acuity improved to 20/20 within two months. Approximately one year later, after discontinuing steroid drops, the patient returned with recurrent symptoms, necessitating an endothelial keratoplasty. At the most recent follow-up two years after surgery, the patient was doing well.

Demographics: 41-year-old male
Chief complaint: Elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels markedly above normal without associated muscle pain or weakness.
History of present illness: The patient has a long-standing history of episodic CK elevation attributed to his occupation and sports activities. In his teens he experienced a systemic parasitic infection. He later developed persistent periorbital and facial swelling with mild erythema and skin thickening, which was unresponsive to retinoids and briefly improved with low-dose steroids. At age 40 he noted hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngeal examination revealed lesions that were found to contain intracellular parasites on histology and PCR. He was treated with intravenous therapy targeting the parasite, after which he developed marked hyperCKemia and an increase in serum creatinine, prompting hospital admission for evaluation of a possible inflammatory muscle disease. Immunologic work-up showed reduced IgG, borderline low IgA, normal to borderline high IgM, decreased CD4/CD8 ratio, and low NK and B-cell numbers. Genetic testing identified a hemizygous missense variant in the gene encoding CD40 ligand. Metabolic evaluation revealed a heterozygous missense variant in a gene associated with fatty-acid oxidation–related muscle stress. He was started on immunoglobulin replacement therapy and received antiparasitic treatment, followed by additional therapy for persistent facial swelling. During follow-up a soft-palate lesion was biopsied and diagnosed as an EBV-associated extranodal lymphoma, for which he received chemotherapy and local radiotherapy, achieving complete remission. He remains on immunoglobulin replacement and prophylactic therapy.

Demographics: 44-year-old male
Chief complaint: High fever

Demographics: 19-year-old male
Chief complaint: severe throat pain and fever
History of present illness: The patient had a 6-month history of throat irritation that progressed over several days to severe throat pain and fever. A third relapse occurred, again with severe uvular erosion and airway edema necessitating tracheotomy; treatment with treatment B and continued immunoglobulin substitution was provided, followed by secondary prophylaxis with an antiprotozoal agent administered intermittently. The patient has remained relapse-free for at least two years while receiving subcutaneous immunoglobulin substitution.

Demographics: 32-year-old male
Chief complaint: Fever, confusion and worsening consciousness progressing to coma
History of present illness: The patient had been traveling in the Democratic Republic of Congo for five months and had not taken malaria chemoprophylaxis. He required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Initial brain CT was unremarkable. Brain MRI performed on day 3 showed diffuse T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the centrum semiovale, periventricular, frontal, occipital white matter and cerebellum, with central micro-hemorrhages on gradient-echo sequences and no post-contrast enhancement. Follow-up MRI on day 15 showed resolution of cerebellar and periventricular lesions and reduction of the remaining white-matter lesions, with small areas of post-contrast enhancement. By day 32 he regained consciousness and was transferred to a rehabilitation unit, but persistent left-sided motor weakness remained at four-month follow-up.

The prostate and residual lung lesions were treated with stereotactic body radiation therapy, and the lymphoid disorder continued on systemic therapy with ongoing metabolic remission.

Demographics: 65-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient reported an insidious onset of left eye visual blurring three years ago that slowly progressed. Neurological examination revealed a left visual field quadrantanopia without papilledema. MRI of the brain demonstrated a pituitary mass measuring approximately 2.0 cm × 1.8 cm × 2.0 cm compressing the left optic chiasm. Baseline neuroendocrine testing showed low cortisol, low growth hormone, and low testosterone with other pituitary hormones within normal limits. He underwent elective trans-sphenoidal surgery without dural breach; the procedure was uneventful and he was extubated thereafter. On postoperative day 1 he developed polyuria and was given desmopressin. On day 7 he became febrile, tachypneic, tachycardic and noted a minimal cough; chest auscultation was clear and chest X-ray showed minimal perihilar haziness. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,000 cells/µL and C-reactive protein 200 mg/L, and empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy was started. The same day he complained of headache and neck pain. On day 9 his Glasgow Coma Scale deteriorated (E4V5M6 to E3V3M5), and he exhibited neck stiffness with positive Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs. White blood cell count rose to 14,000 cells/µL and CRP remained >200 mg/L. Blood cultures drawn on day 7 grew a Gram-negative bacillus identified as Elizabethkingia meningoseptica with carbapenem resistance. He was intubated for hemodynamic instability and transferred to neuro-critical care, where meropenem and ciprofloxacin were added. Lumbar puncture performed on day 9 yielded clear yellowish cerebrospinal fluid with 10 cells/mm³ (predominantly polymorphonuclear cells), glucose 2.2 mmol/L, protein 0.57 g/L, and grew the same organism. Despite antimicrobial therapy, neurological status did not improve, and contrast-enhanced CT of the brain revealed a short-segment thrombus within a midline cerebral venous sinus. Therapeutic anticoagulation with subcutaneous clexane was initiated. On day 13 tracheal aspirate cultured Acinetobacter baumannii that was extensively drug-resistant; polymyxin B was added. The patient completed two weeks of polymyxin, meropenem, and ciprofloxacin, followed by oral levofloxacin for an additional two weeks. He was successfully extubated on day 17, repeat imaging showed resolution of the venous sinus thrombus, inflammatory markers normalized, and he made a full neurological recovery at follow-up.

Demographics: 25-year-old female

She was initially treated with vancomycin, later switched to daptomycin due to subtherapeutic levels, and was discharged to complete a six-week course. Two days after discharge she returned with fever, generalized weakness, recurrent aphasia, and edema around the surgical site. Imaging showed focal dehiscence of the temporal bone, leptomeningeal enhancement of the left cerebral hemisphere, and a complex extra-axial fluid collection. Surgical exploration revealed purulent drainage in multiple intracranial compartments. She received broad-spectrum antibiotics (including daptomycin, cefepime, metronidazole) but worsened neurologically. Repeat imaging displayed extensive leptomeningeal enhancement and swelling in the left frontoparietal region. Continuous EEG monitoring showed electrographic seizure activity without clinical signs. Gram stains from operative specimens showed white blood cells but no organisms; cultures remained negative initially, then produced pinpoint colonies on anaerobic media after several days. The pattern raised suspicion for a fastidious organism, and molecular sequencing identified a Mycoplasma-like species. Therapy was changed to levofloxacin and doxycycline, after which her aphasia improved markedly. She was discharged to complete an eight-week course of levofloxacin, a six-week course of doxycycline, and a six-week course of daptomycin. Follow-up MRI one month after completing antibiotics showed resolution of edema and leptomeningeal enhancement, and she remained symptom-free. Eleven months later she underwent autologous cranioplasty and recovered well.

Demographics: 17-year-old female

History of present illness: The patient presented with several days of fever, asthenia, cough, anorexia, abdominal pain and vomiting. Ten days before hospitalization she had prolonged close contact with a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 case. On admission she was noted to have mild splenomegaly and laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis, markedly elevated ESR and CRP, and increased transaminases and bilirubin. A nasopharyngeal PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. Initial chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Ferritin was mildly increased, while triglycerides, fibrinogen and LDH remained within normal limits. Autoimmune serologies were largely negative except for a low-titer antinuclear antibody. Imaging with CT of the abdomen confirmed hepatomegaly and mild gallbladder wall edema without obstruction; chest CT revealed multiple basal lung nodules and a small pericardial fluid collection. The patient also exhibited painful erythematous lesions on the fingertips that resolved within 24 hours. Despite supportive care her condition worsened, and a repeat CT showed improvement of the pulmonary nodules but new changes in the liver and pancreas, accompanied by rising serum amylase and lipase. Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen showed moderate peri-portal inflammatory infiltrate without bile duct injury. Over the following weeks, treatment led to resolution of fever, normalization of inflammatory markers, and gradual clinical improvement.

Demographics: 67-year-old male

Clinical condition improved, and a repeat abdominal CT three days later showed resolution of the intramural air. He was discharged after respiratory symptoms improved and arranged for outpatient follow-up.

Demographics: 62-year-old woman
Chief complaint: fever with malaise, abdominal discomfort and dark-colored urine
History of present illness: The patient was admitted for consolidation chemotherapy following remission of mixed-phenotype acute leukemia. After a prior hospital stay complicated by two episodes of fever with low white blood cell counts, she was discharged in good condition. Twelve days after discharge she was readmitted for the next chemotherapy cycle. Eleven days into the cycle, she again developed fever while neutropenic and was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. Twenty-five days after starting chemotherapy, while her white blood cell count was 0.06 ×10^9/L, she developed a new febrile episode. Laboratory testing at that time showed a rapid decline in hemoglobin from 8.6 to 6.8 g/dL and elevated unconjugated bilirubin. Within hours she became agitated, somnolent, complained of vague abdominal discomfort, and showed decreasing oxygen saturation. Her urine turned reddish. Repeat labs demonstrated further drop in hemoglobin to 4.5 g/dL, microcytosis, severe metabolic acidosis (pH 7.14), markedly elevated lactate (19.5 mmol/L), and rising creatinine. A contrast-enhanced CT of chest and abdomen revealed an air-dense lesion in the right hepatic lobe and, later, bilateral pulmonary ground-glass consolidations. She required intensive care, vasopressor support, renal replacement therapy, and multiple blood transfusions. Over the subsequent days her respiratory status worsened, prompting high-flow nasal cannula therapy and empiric antifungal treatment. Despite aggressive management, she remained dialysis-dependent and later developed progressive encephalopathy, ultimately leading to death.

Demographics: 86-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient developed fever up to 39.0 °C, chills, fatigue, weakness, and bile-stained vomiting. He was started on broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, but 8 hours later his fever recurred, he developed a severe headache, neck stiffness with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, and his platelet count fell sharply while D-dimer rose markedly. Neurological imaging later revealed intracranial bleeding, and lumbar puncture produced bloody cerebrospinal fluid with high opening pressure. He experienced a generalized seizure requiring anticonvulsant therapy. After initial stabilization, he complained of abdominal distension, poor appetite, and markedly reduced bowel movements, suggestive of markedly decreased intestinal motility. Laboratory studies then showed neutrophilia, rising bilirubin and gamma-glutamyl transferase. Follow-up imaging showed extension of the venous thrombosis into portal vein branches. Anticoagulation therapy was initiated, leading to improvement in bowel symptoms and reduction of the venous thrombosis on subsequent scans. Later, he developed painful redness, swelling, and warmth of both wrists, considered an inflammatory joint reaction, which improved with anti-inflammatory treatment. The overall clinical course improved, and he was discharged after 33 days.

After initial clinical improvement, antibiotics were stopped in the second week, but one week later she developed fever, productive yellow-ish sputum and respiratory distress; chest radiography revealed a right-lung consolidation and she was empirically treated with ciprofloxacin and teicoplanin, leading to improvement. A subsequent left lower-lobe consolidation appeared, prompting a change to ceftazidime. During this period a malar rash recurred, and oral corticosteroids were increased while hydroxychloroquine was restarted. She remained in the ICU until August 2012, was discharged on a tapering steroid regimen and hydroxychloroquine, and later required additional flares treated with cyclophosphamide and B-cell depleting therapy, achieving good response. At 18-month follow-up there were no new severe infections.

Demographics: 51-year-old female
Chief complaint: Dyspnea, dizziness, severe soreness in the right thigh, and difficulty walking
History of present illness: The patient underwent a transobturator mid-urethral sling (TVT-O) procedure with synthetic sling implantation for urinary incontinence one week prior to presentation. Blood glucose monitoring was poor and oral hypoglycemic medication adherence was inconsistent after discharge. Two days post-procedure the urinary catheter was removed. One week later she developed dyspnea, dizziness, marked pain and swelling of the right thigh, and difficulty walking. On examination she had mild redness and swelling of the right inner thigh near the hip, extreme tenderness of the right vaginal wall with an unpleasant odor, but the anterior vaginal wall incision appeared intact with no discharge. Computed tomography of the pelvis and thighs demonstrated multiple deep-tissue gas-filled cavities in the pelvic floor and bilateral thigh muscle roots. The patient received ultrasound-guided drainage of the collection and was started on broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy along with management of metabolic abnormalities and electrolyte balance. Over the ensuing weeks, repeat imaging showed resolution of gas collections, the thigh swelling decreased, and the patient’s symptoms improved, culminating in a full recovery with stable glycemic control and continued urinary continence on follow-up.

Demographics: 8-year-old male

History of present illness: At 34 weeks of pregnancy the patient underwent serologic screening that showed a reactive rapid plasma reagin test at 1:2 dilution and a positive treponemal hemagglutination assay. Both mother and child remain in follow-up.

Demographics: 82-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient had a known enlargement of the aortic arch measuring 68 mm. Demographics: 38-year-old
Chief complaint: decreased vision in the right eye
History of present illness: The patient was started on anticoagulant therapy for inflammation of the retinal vessels. Three weeks later, because the inflammation worsened, a triamcinolone injection was given into the Tenon capsule. A broad-spectrum penicillin preparation was also initiated for a concurrent syphilis infection. About 50 days after the initial visit, new abnormal blood-vessel growth appeared from the optic disc toward the upper retinal vascular arcade, leading to bleeding into the vitreous cavity and a drop in corrected visual acuity of the right eye to 0.02. Fluorescein angiography showed dye leakage from the new vessels and an expansion of non-perfused retinal areas. At three months, laser photocoagulation was applied to the non-perfused retina, but the abnormal vessels persisted and further vitreous re-bleeding occurred. Four months after the first visit, a pars plana vitrectomy was performed because vision had deteriorated to counting fingers. The surgery included core vitrectomy, creation of an artificial posterior detachment, removal of the fibrovascular membrane from the optic disc to the upper retinal arcade, and endophotocoagulation of the ischemic retina while preserving the natural lens. Post-operative testing of vitreous humor and serum confirmed the syphilis infection. Three months after surgery, the abnormal vessels had resolved, leakage on angiography decreased, and visual acuity improved to 0.3.
Exposures risk factors: syphilis infection

Demographics: 19-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient, a 19-year-old male with relapsed Philadelphia chromosome-like B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia who had undergone a haploidentical stem cell transplant, developed fever on post-transplant day +16. Head CT showed a small left frontal intraparenchymal bleed; brain MRI demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions raising concern for septic emboli, and MR angiography was negative for aneurysm. An echocardiogram showed no intracardiac shunt, valve disease, or vegetation. Despite clearance of Bacillus cereus from blood, fever persisted, prompting broadening of antibiotics and empirical trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole because of known T. gondii IgG seropositivity; this was stopped after negative T. gondii PCR from blood, CSF, and BAL. Work-up for fungal and viral pathogens was negative. By day +49 he developed vomiting and diarrhea, leading to endoscopy, which showed only rare apoptotic bodies in duodenum and colon, not supporting graft-versus-host disease. On day +51 he experienced rapid-onset respiratory decline and worsening somnolence. Chest CT revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities, and he required mechanical ventilation and vasoactive support for circulatory instability. He was treated with multiple antimicrobial agents, plasma exchange, and intravenous immunoglobulin for thrombocytopenia-associated organ dysfunction. Demographics: 20-year-old male
Chief complaint: Fever and diarrhea
History of present illness: The patient underwent an unrelated donor peripheral stem cell transplant and was discharged home on post-transplant day 21. Despite ongoing therapy, his inflammatory markers rose further, and he remained critically ill with persistent respiratory failure and catecholamine-refractory hypotension. Care was withdrawn on day 95, and he subsequently died.

Demographics: 59-year-old woman
Chief complaint: productive cough without fever
History of present illness: The patient developed a productive cough in April 2018 without fever. Initial empirical antibiotics (ceftriaxone and tazobactam for 15 days, followed by amoxicillin and metronidazole for 4 weeks) did not resolve the symptoms, which persisted albeit attenuated. Chest CT at that time showed lobar ground-glass opacities with superimposed reticulations and a small patchy area of consolidation in the right middle lobe. No further treatment was given, but occasional coughing continued. In November 2018 she presented with worsening cough; examination was unremarkable and routine laboratory tests were normal. Sputum, blood, and bronchoalveolar lavage cultures and smears were negative. Transbronchial lung biopsy revealed numerous foamy macrophages, cholesterol clefts, multinucleated giant cells, and interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates with fibrosis. She reported frequent use of household spray and hair spray. She was started on oral prednisone with tapering, leading to symptom improvement and discharge. In early April 2019 she returned with a harsher cough and copious yellow sticky sputum. Repeat CT showed progression of the ground-glass opacities to lobar consolidation with air bronchograms in the right middle lobe. Laboratory studies remained largely normal, but high-sensitivity C-reactive protein was 12.32 mg/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 71 mm/h. Interferon-gamma release assay was negative. All microbiological studies, including smears, cultures, (1,3)-β-D-glucan and galactomannan tests, and next-generation sequencing, failed to identify a pathogen. Repeat transbronchial lung biopsy again demonstrated numerous foamy macrophages and granulomatous lesions without caseous necrosis.

Demographics: 44-year-old male
Chief complaint: acute inflammatory lumbar pain
History of present illness: Three months after beginning a standard antimicrobial regimen for a pleural condition, the patient developed acute lumbar pain with marked spinal tenderness and limited motion. He had no respiratory symptoms and a normal neurologic exam. Initial laboratory tests showed mild anemia, normal white cell count, elevated ESR and CRP. Imaging demonstrated vertebral changes at the lower L1 and upper L2 levels and a small left pleural effusion. An MRI revealed vertebral involvement with a fluid collection adjacent to the left psoas muscle. He underwent CT-guided drainage of the collection, which yielded purulent material with negative Gram and acid-fast stains and no bacterial growth. Treatment was prolonged, and a spinal brace was applied. Six months later, the lumbar pain worsened and new soft-tissue fluid collections appeared in the left gluteal and trochanteric regions. The patient was transferred to a specialized unit, and a second-line antimicrobial regimen was started. Over the following months, the collections resolved, inflammatory markers normalized, and the patient gained weight. Follow-up imaging at 12 months showed a vertebral fracture at L1-L2 and near-complete resolution of the fluid collections. The patient completed a prolonged course of therapy, experienced mild peripheral paresthesias managed with vitamins, and was declared cured, now participating in a spinal rehabilitation program.

Demographics: 24-year-old female
Chief complaint: repeated watery diarrhea with abdominal pain and fever
History of present illness: At age 19 the patient developed a rash, oral ulcers, and joint pain; autoantibody testing was positive and she was started on long-term corticosteroids and an antimalarial agent, with gradual tapering. In August 2018 she began to have frequent yellow watery stools (up to ten times daily), abdominal pain, high fevers (up to 40 °C), nausea and loss of appetite. No specific treatment was given initially. She was admitted in October 2018; laboratory tests showed anemia, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, thrombocytosis, positive urinalysis for blood and cells, positive fecal occult blood, and fungal elements on stool smear. Inflammatory markers were markedly elevated. Imaging showed interstitial lung changes. She received pulse corticosteroid therapy and antifungal agents without significant improvement. She was transferred in early November 2018; repeat labs showed worsening anemia, thrombocytopenia, persistent positive urinalysis and occult blood, and high C-reactive protein. CT of the thorax and abdomen demonstrated interstitial lung changes, thickening of the ascending colon wall with surrounding exudate, and multiple calcified lymph nodes. The patient had markedly reduced urine output (~100 mL/day) with cloudy urine. Cystography revealed leakage of contrast from the bladder into the bowel, and renal scintigraphy showed contrast passage into both kidneys and bladder, suggesting a communication between the urinary and gastrointestinal tracts. Colonoscopy identified multiple ulcerations in the colon; biopsy showed chronic inflammation and granulation tissue. Additional testing showed positive interferon-γ release assay, detection of acid-fast bacilli by PCR on colon biopsy, and positive acid-fast staining. Despite ongoing antimicrobial therapy, diarrhea persisted. One month later the patient required gastrointestinal decompression and placement of a small-bowel drainage tube for an acute low-segment intestinal blockage. She was later discharged with clinical improvement.

Demographics: 42-year-old female

History of present illness: The patient noticed gradual loss of vision in the right eye over two weeks without any other systemic symptoms. The patient was started on systemic antimicrobial therapy together with oral corticosteroids, which were tapered over eight weeks. The ocular lesion began to heal from the edges within two weeks of therapy. At ten-month follow-up a scarred lesion remained stable with visual acuity improving to 6/12p. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated patchy hypofluorescence and late leakage. Spectral domain OCT revealed increased foveal thickness, a dome-shaped hyperreflective band at the retinal pigment epithelium level and intraretinal cystic changes. Demographics: 50-year-old female
Chief complaint: Lump in the left breast for one year, painless and gradually enlarging
History of present illness: The patient noticed a painless, slowly enlarging mass in the left breast one year ago. Over time the lesion became hard, irregular, and mobile, measuring approximately 6.0 × 3.0 cm in the lower outer quadrant, with overlying skin puckering and nipple retraction. Two left axillary lymph nodes were palpable and mildly tender. Fine-needle aspiration showed clusters of pleomorphic cells with large nuclei, irregular nuclear membranes, prominent nucleoli, and moderate cytoplasm, consistent with a malignant breast lesion. Cytology of the axillary nodes revealed similar malignant cells. Pre-operative workup included complete blood count (mild microcytic hypochromic anemia), erythrocyte sedimentation rate, chest radiograph, and abdominal ultrasound, all otherwise normal. Demographics: 68-year-old male

History of present illness: The patient had been treated as an unresolved upper respiratory infection with multiple courses of antibiotics without lasting relief. He completed a course of co-amoxiclav and doxycycline shortly before presentation. Over the preceding week his condition worsened with rigors, profuse sweating, an episode of vertigo, oxygen saturation of 89% on room air and temperature of 39 °C. He reported increasing dyspnea, a productive cough that changed from green to clear sputum, and persistent fever. In the emergency department he was febrile, received intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam, paracetamol and fluids, and subsequently developed an irregular cardiac rhythm for which anticoagulation was started. Imaging revealed a sizable fluid collection around the heart and a right-sided pleural fluid collection. Initial microbiology cultures were negative. After an initial improvement he deteriorated again with renewed dyspnea, fever and lung crepitations, prompting a switch to a different broad-spectrum antibiotic and NSAIDs. Laboratory testing showed a positive interferon-gamma release assay. Despite negative PCR and acid-fast stains, a latent infection was considered and a four-drug antimicrobial regimen was initiated (specific agents omitted). Subsequent cardiac imaging demonstrated new regional wall motion abnormalities, septal bounce, and a thickened pericardial structure with organized fluid. Steroids were added temporarily. The patient later underwent surgical removal of the pericardial tissue, after which antimicrobial therapy was adjusted. Post-operatively he experienced a syncopal event with bilateral acute cerebral infarcts and required therapeutic anticoagulation. Follow-up echocardiography showed reduced left ventricular systolic function with an estimated ejection fraction of 40 %. Two months later he was readmitted for lower gastrointestinal bleeding attributed to excess anticoagulation, leading to further modification of his antimicrobial regimen. At three-month outpatient review he reported no new complaints.

Repeat CT demonstrated a loculated pleural collection with new gas formation, raising concern for an infected collection. A second VATS procedure was performed, revealing a large volume of pus within the prior node region, which was evacuated and the cavity irrigated. After the second operation his temperature normalized and laboratory markers returned to baseline. He was discharged eight days later without residual fever or signs of inflammation.

Demographics: 16-year-old male

Aggressive supportive measures including fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, chest tube placement, and continuous renal replacement therapy were instituted. Demographics: 33-year-old Indian male
Chief complaint: Sharp pain in the right testicle radiating to the right buttock, lower back, pelvic region on both sides and perineum, together with daily low-grade fever, chills, excessive sweating, generalized weakness and malaise
History of present illness: From June to November 2016 the patient experienced persistent sharp pain in the right testicle radiating to the right buttock, lower back, both sides of the pelvis and the perineum. He also reported daily low-grade fever (37.5-37.7 °C) with morning chills lasting about 1.5 hours, profuse sweating, generalized weakness and malaise. A urine culture performed during this period was sterile after 48 h of aerobic incubation. KUB ultrasound showed normal kidneys and bladder with no calculi or hydronephrosis, and the prostate appeared to be of normal size. Digital rectal examination by a urologist revealed a tender, boggy prostate. Multiple courses of oral and intravenous antibiotics (azithromycin, doxycycline, ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, amikacin) were given over four months without symptom improvement. In October 2016 a transrectal ultrasound measured the prostate volume at 21.98 ml. In November 2016 the patient traveled to Tbilisi, Georgia, where a full urologic work-up was repeated; cultures of expressed prostatic secretions (EPS) and semen were sterile for fungi and gonococcus, and a low-growth Staphylococcus epidermidis isolate was deemed non-pathogenic. Blood counts, ESR, CRP and PSA were within normal limits. The patient then began a regimen of bacteriophage preparations (oral liquid, rectal suppositories and urethral instillations). After five days his temperature normalized and remained below 37 °C. Testicular and back pain increased briefly after starting the therapy and began to subside after three weeks. Weakness, night sweats and chills gradually decreased. In March 2017 repeat EPS and semen cultures grew Streptococcus mitis, which was resistant to the standard phage preparations; targeted phage therapy was continued. By June 2017 night sweats, chills, excessive sweating and weakness had fully resolved. A custom phage specific for the S. mitis strain was administered from November 2017 to January 2018, after which pelvic and perineal pain further diminished. A repeat transrectal ultrasound in November 2017 showed the prostate volume had decreased to 14.38 ml with no sonographic signs of inflammation. EPS and semen cultures performed in May 2018 were sterile, leukocyte counts in these fluids were normal, and the prostate felt small and firm on rectal palpation. By the end of the observation period the patient reported complete remission of his prior complaints.

Demographics: 56-year-old female
Chief complaint: abdominal distention and generalized malaise
History of present illness: The patient presented with abdominal distention, generalized malaise, mid-back pain radiating to both lower extremities, dysuria, incomplete voiding, and urinary urgency. The patient received systemic antifungal therapy and percutaneous nephrostomy with local antifungal irrigation, leading to clinical and laboratory improvement.
